answers: Chicken giant Tyson Foods says it will retrain all of its workers who deal with live birds after an animal rights group released hidden footage from within its facilities on Wednesday, USA Today reports. According to the Washington Post, the video from Compassion Over Killing shows workers choking, punching, and kicking chickens, plus running them over with forklifts and leaving them in piles to die. One worker in the video says it's "inhumane" to kill a chicken by stepping on its head while he kills a chicken by stepping on its head. Tyson calls the behavior "inexcusable" and says it fired 10 employees at the Virginia facilities shown in the video. Animal rights activists have infiltrated Tyson Foods to film such videos at least five times in a little over a year.

**Summary of News on Tyson Foods and Animal Welfare Allegations**

In late 2016, animal rights group Compassion Over Killing released undercover footage from Tyson Foods facilities in Virginia, revealing severe mistreatment of chickens. The video, filmed by an investigator working undercover, showed workers engaging in violent and inhumane treatment of birds, including stomping, kicking, punching, and suffocating them. Some workers were seen using plastic rods to “bone” chickens, a process that involves inserting the rods into the birds’ beaks, and others were caught leaving injured birds to die in “dead piles.” One worker warned the investigator that such actions could be reported to authorities, stating, “You can’t let nobody see you do that.”

Tyson Foods, the largest chicken-processing company in the U.S., responded by condemning the behavior as “inexcusable” and firing 10 employees depicted in the video. The company also announced the discontinuation of the “boning” process at two of the facilities featured in the video, although it had already phased out the practice at other locations. Tyson’s vice president of sustainable food production, Christine Daugherty, emphasized the company’s commitment to humane treatment of animals and stated that all workers should adhere to proper animal handling protocols.

The allegations are part of a broader pattern of undercover investigations into Tyson’s operations. This is the fifth such incident in roughly 13 months, with activists typically gaining access by working at the facilities and recording footage secretly. Compassion Over Killing, based in Washington, D.C., has previously conducted similar investigations and continues to advocate for improved animal welfare standards in the industry.

The video has also prompted Tyson to retrain all live poultry workers on animal welfare policies and to hold video conferences with senior management to address the issue. The company has also reached out to local authorities in the affected counties, though it has not confirmed whether it seeks criminal charges against the workers involved.

Compassion Over Killing’s executive director, Erica Meier, argued that the abuse is a systemic problem within Tyson and that the company must be held accountable. The group has formally reported the incidents to prosecutors and animal control officials in Mecklenburg, Buckingham, and Lunenburg counties, though no charges have been filed as of the time of the report.
